steps.label: The polynomial classifier
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Made from the lecture lec05-kp15 with view-from-text-v3: pages were planned first and each page is mainly one native infographic (designed in HTML and converted to native nodes), with the terms defined on the same page. 8 pages; every number is computed by program.

steps.label: Second-order expansion
steps.speakerNotes: This is the first page of KP15. The prerequisite is the linear discriminant function and least squares (KP13). A polynomial classifier uses a polynomial of degree at most r as the discriminant, that is, it takes the product terms whose degrees sum to at most r as new coordinates and then learns a linear classifier. With two inputs and second order, g(x) equals w0 plus w1 x1 plus w2 x2 plus w12 x1 x2 plus w11 x1 squared plus w22 x2 squared, 6 terms: 1 bias, 2 linear, 1 interaction and 2 square terms. An interaction term multiplies two or more different inputs. Writing the new coordinates y as [x1, x2, x1x2, x1 squared, x2 squared], g is still linear in the 6 weights, so every linear method from before applies directly. Next, the next page covers solving XOR with the interaction term.

steps.label: XOR and interaction
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the second-order expansion of two inputs. This page uses XOR to see the power of the interaction term. Points (0,0) and (1,1) are class B, (0,1) and (1,0) are class A, and no straight line separates them. Take u equal to x1 minus a half and v equal to x2 minus a half; the discriminant is g equal to a quarter minus 2uv, which in x is minus a quarter plus x1 plus x2 minus 2 x1 x2. The program gives g(0,0), g(0,1), g(1,0), g(1,1) as minus 0.25, 0.75, 0.75, minus 0.25, so g above 0 is A and below 0 is B, all four correct. The left shows the lifted coordinate table and the right the two regions cut by the hyperbola; the boundary is curved in the original coordinates but is a flat plane in the new coordinates. Next, the next page covers the term-count formula.

steps.label: Term-count formula
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on solving XOR with the interaction term. This page gives the term-count formula. A polynomial of l inputs and degree at most r has k equal to C(l plus r, r) terms, that is, (l plus r) factorial over r factorial times l factorial. For l equal to 2 and r from 1 to 5 the counts are 3, 6, 10, 15, 21 (computed by program). For example r equal to 2 is the 6 terms of the previous page. The count comes from enumerating the product terms whose degrees sum to at most r, which equals the number of ways to put r balls into l plus 1 boxes. Next, the next page covers the term explosion and memory.

steps.label: Term explosion
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the term-count formula. This page looks at the term explosion. The left chart is on a log scale with three lines for l equal to 2, 10 and 100 and r from 1 to 10; at l equal to 10 and r equal to 10 there are 184,756 terms. On the right, memory at 8 bytes per number: with 1000 samples the design matrix Φ is 1000 by 184,756, about 1.48 GB; the normal equation of KP13 needs ΦᵀΦ, which is 184,756 by 184,756, about 273 GB, roughly 185 times larger and beyond an ordinary computer. At l equal to 2 and r equal to 10 there are only 66 terms, so the explosion comes from more inputs (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the two-moons experiment.

steps.label: Two moons
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the term explosion and memory. This page uses the two-moons experiment. The training set has 30 points per class, 60 in all: class A on the upper half circle, class B on the shifted lower half circle, each with noise 0.2; the test set has 500 points per class from another seed. For r from 1 to 5, the terms, training accuracy and new-point accuracy (computed by program): r equal to 1 is 3 terms, 78.3% and 84.9%; r equal to 3 is 10 terms, 90.0% and 93.2%. The solid curve is the boundary at r equal to 3 and the dashed line is r equal to 1; the curved boundary follows the two crescents while the line cannot. Next, the next page covers degree and overfitting.

steps.label: Overfitting
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the two-moons experiment. This page raises the degree to 10. On the same two-moons data, the terms, training and new-point accuracy for r from 1 to 10 (computed by program): r equal to 5 is 21 terms, 96.7% and 91.2%; r equal to 8 is 36 terms, 98.3% and 92.0%; r equal to 9 is 55 terms, 100% and 63.7%; r equal to 10 is 66 terms, 100% and 55.5%. Overfitting: the model has room to memorize every training point, noise included, so training reaches 100% while new points are near random guessing; 55 terms at r equal to 9 and 66 at r equal to 10 already approach or exceed the 60 training points. The condition number is the factor by which a matrix magnifies small errors: 3.25 at r equal to 1, 3.44×10⁴ at r equal to 6, 4.42×10⁶ at r equal to 8 and 8.72×10⁸ at r equal to 10, so the solution becomes less and less stable. Next, the next page covers the kernel preview.

steps.label: Kernel preview
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on degree and overfitting. This page previews the kernel method; the details are in KP19. Take l equal to 2, second order, x equal to (1, 2) and z equal to (3, minus 1). Directly: the square of (1 plus x·z), where x·z is 3 minus 2 equal to 1, so (1 plus 1) squared is 4. With the new coordinates and term-by-term products: φ(x) equals (1, √2 x1, √2 x2, x1 squared, x2 squared, √2 x1x2), and the products of φ(x) and φ(z) term by term are 1, 6, minus 4, 9, 4, minus 12, which also sum to 4 (computed by program). The results agree, but the left side needs only one inner product and one square; at l equal to 10 and r equal to 10 it costs the same and never expands 184,756 terms. Next, the next page covers the exercises.

steps.label: Exercises
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the kernel preview. Two exercises. Q1: how many terms with 4 inputs and degree at most 3? k equals C(4 plus 3, 3) equals C(7, 3), which is 7 factorial over 3 factorial times 4 factorial, that is 5040 over 6 times 24, equal to 35 terms; check: 35 is C(7, 3). Q2: with g equal to minus a quarter plus x1 plus x2 minus 2 x1 x2, which class is the point (1.5, 1.5) (g above 0 is A)? g(1.5, 1.5) equals minus 0.25 plus 3 minus 4.5, equal to minus 1.75, which is below 0, so class B; check: the point lies in the upper-right B region, the same region as (1,1) (computed by program). That ends this unit; next, move on to the next unit.
